title: Contingency contracting basics (for 51Cs)
summary: 51Cs exist to deploy. A contingency contracting officer (CCO) buys what forces need in the field, often fast and far from home, using the same rules plus emergency flexibilities. Speed never replaces authority, funds, competition where possible and a good file.
why: The exam does not test contingency contracting directly, but it is the heart of the 51C job, and the same fundamentals apply under pressure.

sections.body: Most 51Cs serve in Army Contracting Command units such as contracting support brigades and contingency contracting battalions and teams, supporting installations at home and forces overseas. Expect exercises, deployments and humanitarian missions as well as everyday installation buying.

- **Field ordering officers (FOOs)** and **paying agents (PAs):** trained, appointed people who make small purchases and pay cash in the field under strict controls.
- **SF 44:** a purchase order, invoice and voucher in one, for small over-the-counter buys where the supplies are delivered on the spot.
- **Government purchase card** where it is accepted.
- **Requirements review boards:** in theater, commanders often must approve requirements before contracting buys them.
- **Theater business clearance and contractor accountability:** contractors supporting forces overseas follow special clauses, and their personnel are tracked in SPOT (DFARS 225.770).

- Only warranted contracting officers bind the Government; FOOs act within tight written limits.
- Funds must fit the purpose, the time and the amount.
- Compete whenever practical; urgency is an exception to justify, not a habit.
- Host-nation laws and status of forces agreements can affect what you can buy and how.
- FAR Part 19 set-asides are optional outside the United States (FAR 19.000(b)).
- Combating trafficking in persons rules apply to every contract (FAR 22.17).
- Document decisions as you go; files from deployments are audited later.

The Defense Contingency Contracting Handbook (DPCAP website), your unit's standing procedures, WarU's Foundational and Advanced Contingency Contracting credentials (CCON 014B, CCON 015A) and the Barda Bridge simulation (CON 0390).

example.title: Day three of an exercise
example.body: Forty Soldiers arrive at a training site with no working generator. Under the exercise's contingency determination the micro-purchase threshold is $40,000 overseas. A local vendor has a generator for $11,500. You confirm funds, check that the price is reasonable against two other vendors you called, buy it with proper documentation, and note it for the after-action report.

remember: Higher thresholds need a determination: no determination, no higher threshold.
Fast and documented beats fast and lost.
mistakes: Using contingency thresholds without a determination covering the buy.
Letting a FOO or paying agent exceed written limits.
verify: Contingency procedures, FOO and paying agent rules, and local thresholds differ by theater and command. Learn your unit's standing procedures and confirm with your contracting officer.

title: The systems you will use
summary: Contracting runs on a handful of Government systems: SAM.gov for vendors, notices and contract data; PIEE for invoices, contract documents and appointments; your contract writing system; CPARS for performance; and VCE for Army contract files and warrants. Ask for accounts in your first week.
why: You cannot work actions without them, and some roles take weeks to approve.

sections.body:
- **Entity registration:** contractors must be registered before award (FAR 4.203).
- **Exclusions:** check that a contractor is not suspended or debarred before award and before exercising options.
- **Contract Opportunities:** where you post notices and solicitations.
- **Contract data:** award reporting moved into SAM.gov when FPDS.gov was retired in February 2026.

- **Contract writing system:** the Army's is ACWS, which replaced older systems; some offices may still use PD2 during the transition.
- **VCE (Virtual Contracting Enterprise):** Army contract files in the Paperless Contract File, and the warrant application process (VCE-Warrants).
- **CPARS:** contractor performance assessments.
- **SPRS:** supplier risk information, including cybersecurity assessment scores.
- **eSRS:** small business subcontracting reports.
- **GFEBS:** the Army's financial system, where purchase requests and funds live.
- **WarU learning system, AITAS and ATRRS, and CAMP:** your own training and career records.

example.title: The two-week wait
example.body: A new specialist starts in March but cannot release a single solicitation until April because nobody requested a contract writing system role. The fix is simple: on day one, ask your supervisor for the list of systems and roles your office uses and submit every request that week.

remember: SAM for vendors, notices and contract data; PIEE for invoices, documents and appointments.
Request system roles in your first week.
mistakes: Awarding without checking SAM registration and exclusions.
Sharing a CAC or a password to get around a missing role.
verify: System names and roles change and differ by office. Your supervisor will tell you which ones you need.

title: How to pass CON 3990V
summary: Study the way the exam is built: weight your time by the official question counts, memorize the 20 FAR part titles, read FAR Part 15 closely, practice under real conditions, and take the exam at a test center when you are consistently above 75% in practice.
why: In FY26, 79% passed on their first try and the average score was 74.8%, just above the 70% line. A plan moves you from the edge to a comfortable pass.

sections.body:
- Guiding Principles: 42 questions (Contract Principles alone is 18).
- Award: 40 questions, 10 each on price or cost analysis, negotiation, source selection and protests.
- Post-Award: 38 questions.
- Pre-Award: 30 questions.
Spend your time in roughly that proportion, and more on your weakest area.

The exam FAQ says learning the FAR part titles has proven highly effective, and that many questions stem from FAR Part 15. Use the Flashcards deck and FAR Part Match daily until the titles are automatic, and read Part 15 (Contracting by Negotiation) start to finish at least once.

- Take CON 3910: its practice exam is built by the exam's owners.
- Use this guide's exam simulator: closed book, timed, no phone.
- Review every miss: read the explanation and the lesson it links to.
- Use spaced repetition: a little every day beats a long session once a week.

- Read the last sentence first, so you know what is being asked.
- Watch for NOT, EXCEPT, FIRST, BEST and MOST.
- Cross out answers that are clearly wrong, then choose between the rest.
- Answers with absolute words like always or never are often wrong, but not always: check them against the rule.
- If two answers both look right, pick the one that matches the FAR's wording and process most closely.
- Answer every question; there is no penalty for guessing.

Schedule at a Pearson test center if you can (test centers pass about 4% more). Sleep, eat, and arrive early with a government-issued photo ID matching your profile. Pace yourself at about 72 seconds a question and flag the hard ones for later. If you do not pass, you will see your score in each area: use it, take CON 3900V, and try again after 30 days.

example.title: A four-week finish
example.body: Week 1: the 20 part titles and every Guiding Principles lesson. Week 2: Award lessons, price analysis practice and FAR Part 15. Week 3: Post-Award and Pre-Award lessons, plus CON 3910. Week 4: two full exam simulations, reviewing every miss, then the real exam at a test center.

remember: Blueprint, part titles, Part 15, practice, test center.
Aim for 75% or better in practice before you book the exam.
mistakes: Studying only the topics you enjoy.
Taking the exam online on a government computer that blocks the software.
